PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 4

Cosmological distances

The Universe does not have the static Euclidean geometry we’re all familiar with, and on cosmological scales this makes both defining and measuring distances decidedly tricky. The Universe is expanding, and spacetime may also be curved, so much of our usual intuition does not apply. Instead we must take a relativistic view in order to establish how observables (such as the brightness or physical size of distant objects) are related to physical distances. To do this we must consider the metric, which describes the relationship between distance and co-ordinates in four-dimensional spacetime111 You have come across metrics before – for example the Minkowski metric of special relativity – but may not have seen them presented as such..

The metric which describes a homogeneous, isotropic, expanding spacetime is the Robertson-Walker metric (sometimes called the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric), which can be written as follows:

d⁢s2=-c2⁢d⁢t2+a⁢(t)2⁢[d⁢r21-k⁢r2+r2⁢(d⁢θ2+sin2⁡θ⁢d⁢ϕ2)] (1)

This relates the spacetime separation d⁢s (essentially the magnitude of a relativistic 4-vector) to the time co-ordinate t and the three spatial co-ordinates (r,θ,ϕ)222 As the Universe is isotropic, it makes sense to work in spherical co-ordinates. However, if there is no curvature (i.e., k=0) then the term inside the square brackets is simply the polar equivalent of the length element in the more familiar Cartesian co-ordinates: d⁢r2+r2⁢d⁢θ2+r2⁢sin2⁡θ⁢d⁢ϕ2=d⁢x2+d⁢y2+d⁢z2 (2) . d⁢t is the cosmological proper time (often shortened to the “cosmic time”), while the spatial co-ordinates (r,θ,ϕ) are co-moving co-ordinates. This is therefore the (special relativity) Minkowski metric with two corrections: the scale-factor outside the square brackets accounts for the expansion of the Universe; while the first term inside the square brackets accounts for the curvature of spacetime333 Indeed, if we set a⁢(t)=1 and k=0 we recover the Minkowski metric immediately.,444 Note also that isotropy means the curvature term can only act on the radial co-ordinate..

As with many problems in relativity, the tricky part is how to relate physical distances (proper distances, in relativistic parlance) to the distances we can actually measure. There are two common ways to measure distances in astronomy:

  • •

    Look at an object of known brightness and measure how bright it appears to us, then use the inverse-square law to determine its distance.

  • •

    Measure the angular size (on the sky) of an object of known physical size, and use trigonometry to determine how far away it is.

In flat, non-expanding space (i.e., in the local Universe) these two distances are equal, and both equal to the proper distance, but on cosmological scales they are not. The first is referred to as the luminosity distance (denoted dL), while the second is referred to as the angular-diameter distance (dA), and we now consider each in turn. For simplicity we will only consider the case of a flat Universe (k=0) here; including curvature makes the analysis slightly more complex, but doesn’t change the results greatly.

Luminosity distance

We define the (intrinsic) luminosity of our object to be L, and the flux we observe to be F. If the object is at a physical (proper) distance d, in flat, static space these are related by the inverse-square law

F=L4⁢π⁢d2 (3)

where the denominator is simply the area of a sphere of radius d. The luminosity distance is therefore defined (from the observables) as

dL=L4⁢π⁢F (4)

On cosmological scales, however, the expansion of the Universe changes the relationship between L and F. Recalling that L is energy per unit time, while F is energy per unit time per unit area, there are two effects which change the relationship:

  • •

    the individual photons lose energy due to the expansion of space. Essentially photons have their wavelengths ‘‘stretched’’ (redshifted) by a factor555 We will prove this relationship between a and z in the next lecture, but for now I will simply assert it as fact and move on. a⁢(t)=1/(1+z).

  • •

    photons arrive less frequently (due to the increased travel time), also by a factor a⁢(t)=1/(1+z).

If we now define the physical distance to the object to be dp, the relationship between L and F becomes

F=L4⁢π⁢dp2⁢(1+z)2 (5)

Substituting for L (or F) in Equation 4 the luminosity distance is therefore

dL=dp⁢(1+z) (6)

This may also be written as

dL=a0⁢r0⁢(1+z) (7)

where a0 is the scale factor and r0 the co-moving distance (where the 0 subscripts indicate that dp=a0⁢r0 is measured at the present time, and is therefore a proper distance).

In practice F is readily measured (as is z), but for most objects we have no way of knowing the intrinsic luminosity L. Measuring distances in this manner in astronomy relies on us understanding enough astrophysics to know the intrinsic luminosity of some types of astronomical objects; these are often referred to as “standard candles”.

Angular-diameter distance

The other common way to measure distances in astronomy is to measure the spatial extent of objects with known size (so-called “standard rulers”). If an object of (proper) length l is placed perpendicular to the line of sight, at (proper) distance d, we will observe it to have an angular size666 We have used the small-angle approximation sin⁡θ≃θ here (θ≪1). Astronomical sources are small enough that this is almost always valid (even the Sun and Moon are only ≃0.5∘ in angular size). d⁢θ=l/d. The angular-diameter distance is therefore defined as

dA=ld⁢θ (8)

To derive an expression for the cosmological angular-diameter distance, we must use the Robertson-Walker metric (again for the case k=0). Consider a standard ruler of proper length l, placed at a co-moving distance r0. For convenience we orient the “ruler” in the θ-direction (so the distance between its ends has d⁢r=0 and d⁢ϕ=0). As l is a proper length we must consider the metric at the time the light from the ruler was emitted, te, and we observe both ends at the same time so d⁢t=0. From Equation 1 we therefore have

d⁢s2=l2=a⁢(te)2⁢r02⁢d⁢θ2 (9)

and therefore

l=a⁢(te)⁢r0⁢d⁢θ (10)

Recalling that a⁢(t)=1/(1+z), if the ruler has redshift z, then a⁢(te)=a0/(1+z) (where we again use 0 subscripts indicate values at the present time), so

l=a0⁢r01+z⁢d⁢θ (11)

We then substitute into Equation 8 to find

dA=a0⁢r01+z=dp1+z (12)

The relationship between luminosity distance and angular diameter distance (for k=0) is therefore777 Remember that this analysis is for case of a k=0 (flat) Universe. In the more general case there is an additional curvature term alongside the (1+z) terms in all these equations.

dA=dL(1+z)2 (13)

As expected, in the nearby Universe (z≪1) these are equivalent, and equal to the physical distance dp. However, at larger distances they diverge significantly, and for z≫1 the angular-diameter distance decreases with increasing redshift. This gives rise to the highly counter-intuitive result that in the distant Universe, objects appear bigger as they move further away!
